instruction: A website returns HTTP 502 from the load balancer but the backend appears up. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v https://app.example.com/health
curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:<backend-ip> https://app.example.com/health
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
ss -tlnp | grep <backend-port>
**Interpretation:** 502 means the proxy could not get a valid response from the upstream. Hitting the backend directly with --resolve succeeds or fails; if it fails, the upstream is down or on the wrong port. Nginx logs 'connect() failed' or 'upstream prematurely closed'.
**Fix:** Fix the backend (start the service, correct the upstream port/address). If the app crashes on the request, fix the exception. Update the proxy upstream and reload: `nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx`.

instruction: curl returns 'Empty reply from server'. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v http://host/
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host
sudo tcpdump -ni any port 80
sudo journalctl -u <service> -n 50
**Interpretation:** 'Empty reply' means TCP connected but the server closed without an HTTP response. This is typical of a service not speaking HTTP on that port (HTTPS on port 80, IMAP, gRPC) or an app crash before writing headers.
**Fix:** Confirm the protocol and port. Use `curl https://` if TLS is required, or point at the correct port. Fix the app crash revealed in the service logs, then retest with `curl -v`.

instruction: A reverse proxy returns 504 Gateway Timeout intermittently. Diagnose upstream latency.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -w '@curl-format.txt' -o /dev/null -s https://app.example.com/slow
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
grep proxy_read_timeout /etc/nginx/*.conf
**Interpretation:** 504 means the upstream did not respond within proxy_read_timeout. If the backend log shows slow queries, the app is the bottleneck. If the app responds fast when hit directly, the proxy timeout is too low or a connection-pool wait is happening.
**Fix:** Speed up the backend (query optimization, caching) or raise `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_connect_timeout` in nginx, then reload. Add health checks and scale the backend if load-related.

instruction: Users get 301 redirect loops when visiting https://example.com. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -sIL https://example.com
curl -sI http://example.com
sudo nginx -T | grep -i return
**Interpretation:** A loop occurs when both the HTTP and HTTPS vhosts redirect to each other, or the app checks X-Forwarded-Proto incorrectly (sees http behind a TLS-terminating LB and redirects to https, which redirects again).
**Fix:** Ensure only the HTTP server redirects; the HTTPS server serves content. Set `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;` on the terminating LB so the app does not re-redirect. Test with `curl -sIL` and confirm a single 301 then 200.

instruction: An API returns HTTP 401 even though the client sends an Authorization header. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://api.example.com/v1/me
sudo tcpdump -A -ni any port 443 | grep -i authorization
**Interpretation:** If the header appears in curl -v but tcpdump does not show it, it was stripped by a proxy. If it arrives, the server rejected the token (expired, wrong audience/signature). Check the WWW-Authenticate response header.
**Fix:** Ensure proxies forward the Authorization header (`proxy_set_header Authorization $http_authorization;`). Refresh/reissue the token and validate issuer/audience/expiry on the server. Verify clock skew on the auth host.

instruction: A service returns gzip-encoded data with the wrong Content-Length causing truncated responses. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v --compressed https://example.com/big.json -o out.json
curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' https://example.com/big.json
wc -c out.json
gzip -t out.json
**Interpretation:** Mismatched Content-Length vs actual body usually means a proxy or app sets the length of the uncompressed body while sending compressed data, or uses chunked encoding incorrectly. Clients truncate or error.
**Fix:** Remove the manual Content-Length when using gzip; let the server emit chunked encoding or set the compressed length. In nginx ensure `gzip on;` with `gzip_vary on;` and correct proxying, then reload.

instruction: A health check endpoint returns 200 to curl but the load balancer marks the node unhealthy. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v http://localhost/health
curl -v http://<node-ip>/health
curl -v -H 'Host: app.example.com' http://<node-ip>/health
ss -tlnp | grep 80
**Interpretation:** The LB may check a different Host header, path, port, or IP family. If localhost works but the node IP does not, the app may be bound to source-restricted addresses or a firewall allows only the LB subnet.
**Fix:** Make the health endpoint answer the LB's Host/path and ensure the listener binds the node IP. Allow the LB subnet in the firewall, and align IPv4/IPv6. Verify with `curl -H 'Host: app.example.com' http://<node-ip>/health`.

instruction: HTTP responses have high TTFB but fast download. Diagnose server-side processing.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} conn:%{time_connect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com/
strace -p <app-pid> -f -tt -T 2>&1 | head
**Interpretation:** Large `time_starttransfer` with small connect time means the server takes long to produce the first byte: slow application code, DB query, or autoscaling cold start. If the same endpoint is cached and fast, the delay is backend work.
**Fix:** Profile the endpoint, add caching, optimize the DB query, or pre-warm the app. Consider a reverse-proxy cache for static/slow responses and horizontally scale.

instruction: Mixed HTTP/HTTPS content causes browser warnings. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -s https://example.com/page | grep -o 'http://[^" ]*'
grep -rn 'http://' /var/www/html --include=*.html | head
**Interpretation:** If the HTML references http:// resources, browsers block or warn on mixed content. Identify every insecure URL emitted by templates or configs.
**Fix:** Change all resource URLs to https:// or protocol-relative //, or use a Content-Security-Policy with `upgrade-insecure-requests`. Update app templates and re-deploy; verify no http:// remains with the grep above.

instruction: A web server returns 413 Request Entity Too Large for uploads. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v -F 'file=@big.bin' https://example.com/upload
grep -r client_max_body_size /etc/nginx/
php -i | grep upload_max_filesize 2>/dev/null
**Interpretation:** 413 comes from the proxy before the app: nginx default client_max_body_size is 1m. If a PHP/Apache app also has a limit, the app returns its own error after the proxy passes.
**Fix:** Raise nginx `client_max_body_size 100m;` (http/server/location), and matching limits (`upload_max_filesize`, `post_max_size`, Apache LimitRequestBody). Reload and retest with curl.

instruction: HTTP security headers are missing when going through a CDN. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i -E 'strict-transport|content-security|x-frame'
curl -sI --resolve <origin-ip>:443 https://example.com | grep -i -E 'strict-transport|x-frame'
**Interpretation:** If the origin sends the headers but the CDN response lacks them, the CDN is caching an old response or stripping headers. Check the cache HIT status in headers.
**Fix:** Purge the CDN cache and configure it to forward/preserve the headers, or add them at the CDN edge. Set correct Cache-Control so header changes propagate. Verify with a cache-busting query string.

instruction: An HTTP/2 site fails for some clients but HTTP/1.1 works. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v --http2 https://example.com
curl -v --http1.1 https://example.com
openssl s_client -alpn h2 -connect example.com:443
**Interpretation:** If HTTP/1.1 works but HTTP/2 fails, ALPN negotiation or an intermediary is broken. s_client showing no 'ALPN protocol: h2' means the server does not advertise h2, or a firewall mangles the larger setup.
**Fix:** Enable h2 in the server (`listen 443 ssl http2;` in nginx), ensure TLS supports ALPN, and verify no middlebox breaks it. As a stopgap, configure clients to use HTTP/1.1.

instruction: curl to a URL returns 403 from a WAF but the same request works from a browser. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v -A 'Mozilla/5.0' https://example.com/
curl -v https://example.com/
curl -v https://example.com/ -H 'Accept: text/html'
**Interpretation:** WAFs often block the default curl User-Agent or requests lacking browser-like headers/cookies. The 403 body may name the rule or reference a challenge page.
**Fix:** Send a realistic User-Agent and headers in legitimate automation, or whitelist your client IP/service account in the WAF. For APIs, use proper auth headers. Do not bypass the WAF against policy; fix the detection rule with the WAF owner.

instruction: A website is slow only on the first request and fast afterward. Diagnose connection reuse.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -w 'connect:%{time_connect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com/
curl -w 'connect:%{time_connect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com/
ss -tlnp | grep 443
**Interpretation:** First-request slowness with fast subsequent requests means connection setup (DNS, TCP, TLS) dominates. Without keep-alive, every request pays the handshake cost. TLS session resumption also helps.
**Fix:** Enable HTTP keep-alive on client and server, use connection pooling, and enable TLS session tickets/resumption. For servers behind a proxy, ensure upstream keep-alive is on. Confirm connect time drops to near zero on reuse.

instruction: An HTTP response includes the wrong Content-Type causing JSON parse errors. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -sI https://api.example.com/data
curl -s https://api.example.com/data | file -
**Interpretation:** If the body is JSON but Content-Type is text/html or text/plain, clients that trust the header mis-parse it. This often comes from a proxy mapping or a framework default.
**Fix:** Set the correct `Content-Type: application/json` in the app, or force it in nginx for the location. Clear any proxy override and reload. Verify with `curl -sI`.

instruction: HTTP requests fail only when using a proxy. Diagnose proxy configuration.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v -x http://proxy:3128 https://example.com
curl -v --noproxy '*' https://example.com
env | grep -i proxy
cat /etc/environment | grep -i proxy
**Interpretation:** If direct works and proxied fails, the proxy env vars or auth are wrong. Common issues: HTTPS tunneling (CONNECT) blocked, missing Proxy-Authorization, or NO_PROXY not covering internal hosts.
**Fix:** Set correct `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`no_proxy` (include internal CIDRs and localhost), provide credentials, and ensure the proxy allows CONNECT to 443. Verify with `curl -v -x` returning '200 Connection established'.

instruction: A redirect goes to an internal hostname unreachable by clients. Diagnose the Location header.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -sI https://example.com/login
curl -sI https://example.com/api
curl -sI -o /dev/null -w '%{redirect_url}\n' https://example.com/login
**Interpretation:** A 302 Location pointing at an internal name (e.g http://app-server/) leaks backend topology and breaks clients that cannot resolve it. This comes from app config using the upstream Host or a hardcoded internal URL.
**Fix:** Configure the app to emit the public hostname in redirects (set `X-Forwarded-Host` and use it, or an explicit external URL setting). Update the proxy to preserve Host and reload. Verify the Location is the public URL.

instruction: A large file download stalls at a specific percentage. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -o /dev/null https://example.com/big.iso
wget -c https://example.com/big.iso
sudo tcpdump -ni any host example.com and tcp
ss -tni dst <server-ip>
**Interpretation:** A stall at the same offset each time points to a bad cached object at a CDN/proxy, a corrupted upstream file, or an MTU/loss issue. `ss -tni` shows retransmits and a shrinking window if loss.
**Fix:** Purge the CDN/proxy cache and re-fetch from origin to confirm. If loss-related, fix MTU/loss (see fragmentation). Validate the file checksum after download.

instruction: A web app works over HTTP but not HTTPS after installing a certificate. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
curl -v https://example.com
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
sudo nginx -t
journalctl -u nginx -n 30
ss -tlnp | grep 443
**Interpretation:** If curl gets a TLS error or connection reset, the certificate/key is wrong, the chain is incomplete, or the server did not reload after adding the vhost. `nginx -t` and logs reveal an SSL config error.
**Fix:** Fix the cert/key paths and ensure the full chain (leaf + intermediates) is served. If bind to 443 failed, resolve the conflict. Test with `nginx -t` then `systemctl reload nginx`, and verify with `openssl s_client`.

instruction: API responses are randomly truncated under load. Diagnose.
output:
**Diagnose:**
for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' https://api.example.com/data; done
ss -s
dmesg | grep -i -E 'conntrack'
tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
**Interpretation:** Random truncation under load can be a full conntrack table dropping flows, an overloaded app, or a proxy buffer/timeout. dmesg 'nf_conntrack: table full' confirms kernel flow drops.
**Fix:** Raise `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max` and reduce timeout values, or fix the underlying capacity issue (scale the app, raise worker connections). Add response buffering where appropriate and monitor for truncation.
